USA Today reported that some stores were already short of pennies and rounding cash totals to five cents.
description_long: The U.S. Mint struck its final penny for circulation on November 12, 2025, following President Trump’s directive to stop producing the coin. The milestone ended the minting of new one-cent pieces, but pennies already in the public’s hands remain legal tender and retain their value. USA Today reported that some stores had begun running short and rounding cash transactions when customers lacked exact change. The cost of coin production was central to the decision: a penny cost about 3.7 cents to make in fiscal year 2024, while a nickel cost about 13.8 cents. That difference means shifting cash transactions toward nickels could offset some federal savings. The Mint’s final production day did not immediately remove pennies from circulation; an estimated 300 billion remained in use. The end of minting therefore began a gradual change in cash commerce, with retailers and customers adjusting as available pennies diminish.

Meta moved its trust and safety teams from California to Texas, elevated longtime Republican insider Joel Kaplan to head of global policy, removed special restrictions on Trump's accounts imposed after January 6, and dropped content limits on immigration and gender identity discussions — moves Bloomberg described as aimed at an audience of one as Zuckerberg sought to mend fences with the incoming administration. Musk, having acquired Twitter/X in 2022 for $44 billion, had already dismantled most of the platform's content moderation infrastructure and reinstated thousands of suspended far-right accounts; in 2025, X became the primary platform for White House messaging while Musk served in the administration. The simultaneous capitulations of Meta and X — the two largest social media platforms in the world — removed institutional misinformation safeguards covering the majority of Americans' online news consumption just as the Trump administration began its second term.
